title: Kinetic Theory of Gases — Postulates Mapped to Consequences
notes: The postulate → consequence mapping: each idealisation of the kinetic theory, what it explains, and which real-gas failure it causes. A different cut through the material from the main postulates note.
• 'Molecules are point masses (negligible volume)' → explains compressibility and large empty space → fails at high pressure (free volume < container volume, real PV > nRT).

• 'No intermolecular attraction except during collision' → explains indefinite expansion and Dalton's partial pressures → fails near liquefaction (attraction lowers observed pressure, real Z < 1) and is the reason gases condense at all.

• 'Collisions perfectly elastic' → kinetic energy redistributed, not lost; gas temperature stays constant in a rigid container → fails slightly (real collisions excite vibrations; polyatomic gases need internal degrees of freedom for their specific heats).

• 'Random straight-line motion, huge numbers' → statistics (Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution) explains steady macroscopic pressure from microscopic chaos → fails for very low densities where molecule counts fluctuate.
• 'KE ∝ T' → defines absolute temperature microscopically: KE = (3/2)kT per molecule, (3/2)RT per mole → explains why T must be kelvin and why all gases share the same R.

$PV=\frac{1}{3}mn\bar{c}^{2}$ (pressure from momentum transfer) + KE ∝ T (postulate) → $PV=nRT$ → Boyle's, Charles' and Avogadro's laws fall out immediately. One set of postulates explains *all* the gas laws at once — the model's greatest virtue.
### What the model explains beyond the laws

Graham's diffusion/effusion (r ∝ 1/√M), Dalton's partial pressures (independent molecules), Graham's law of effusion, viscosity (momentum transfer between layers) and Brownian-motion style randomness of molecular speeds.
### Where the idealisations bite (recap for exams)

High P: molecular volume matters. Low T / near Tc: attraction matters. Polyatomic gases: rotation/vibration. Very light gases at low T: quantum effects. Liquid state: attraction and volume together — outside the model entirely.
confusion: ❌ 'Negligible molecular volume' is a minor technicality. ✅ It is one of the two postulates whose failure defines all real-gas deviation (the other is no attraction).
❌ Kinetic theory explains why gases liquefy. ✅ It cannot — liquefaction comes from the attractive forces it assumes away; that requires the van der Waals model.
❌ Elastic collisions mean molecules never exchange energy. ✅ They exchange freely but the *total* KE is conserved.

universalFacts: Every postulate is an idealisation — the model is defined by what it ignores.
The pressure equation was derived by Clausius (1857); Maxwell gave the speed distribution in 1860.
The two failed idealisations reappear as the van der Waals constants b (volume) and a (attraction).
examples: **Problem:** Which postulate fails when a gas is compressed to 200 atm? **Solution:** 'molecular volume is negligible' — the molecules' own volume is no longer negligible against the container volume, so the free space shrinks and observed pressure exceeds the ideal prediction (Z > 1).
importantNotes: Learn the postulates as a cause–effect chain; examiners award marks for linking postulate → law → limitation.
Quote the two 'failure postulates' explicitly in any limitations answer.

summary: This view of the kinetic theory maps each postulate to what it explains and to the real-gas failure it causes: negligible molecular volume explains compressibility but fails at high pressure when free volume shrinks below the container volume; no intermolecular attraction explains indefinite expansion and Dalton's partial pressures but fails near liquefaction and is precisely why gases condense; perfectly elastic collisions mean energy is redistributed rather than lost but fail slightly for polyatomic gases, which store energy in rotation and vibration; random motion in huge numbers explains steady pressure from microscopic chaos; and KE ∝ T defines absolute temperature and the shared constant R. The chain PV = ⅓mnc̄² plus KE ∝ T gives PV = nRT and with it all the gas laws at once.
importantConcepts: Postulate-to-consequence mapping: each idealisation explains a gas law and also causes a specific failure
Negligible molecular volume — explains compressibility, fails at high pressure with real PV > nRT
No intermolecular attraction — explains indefinite expansion and partial pressures, fails near liquefaction with real Z < 1
Perfectly elastic collisions — energy redistributed not lost, incomplete for polyatomic specific heats
Random motion of a very large number of molecules — statistics give steady macroscopic pressure
KE ∝ T defining absolute temperature, with (3/2)kT per molecule and (3/2)RT per mole

PV = ⅓mnc̄² combined with KE ∝ T yields PV = nRT, from which Boyle's, Charles' and Avogadro's laws follow immediately.
One set of postulates explains all the gas laws at once, which is the model's greatest virtue.

keyPoints: Learn the postulates as a cause-and-effect chain; examiners award marks for postulate → law → limitation.
Quote the two 'failure postulates' explicitly in any limitations answer: negligible volume and no attraction.
At 200 atm the volume postulate fails, because molecular volume is no longer negligible and Z > 1.
Near the critical temperature the attraction postulate fails, and the attraction term is what allows liquefaction.
Elastic collisions mean molecules exchange energy freely, but the total kinetic energy is conserved.
specialNotes: High pressure: molecular volume matters, so the observed pressure exceeds the ideal prediction and Z > 1.
Low temperature and near the critical point: attraction matters, so the observed pressure is lower and Z < 1.
For polyatomic gases, energy stored in rotation and vibration means the simple theory cannot reproduce their specific heats.
For very light gases at low temperature, quantum effects invalidate the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution the theory assumes.
The liquid state, where attraction and volume act together, lies entirely outside the model.
examShortTricks: Structure any answer as postulate → what it explains → where it fails; that chain is what earns the marks.
The two failure postulates are 'negligible molecular volume' and 'no intermolecular forces' — quote both.
Map: volume postulate → compressibility → fails at high P; attraction postulate → expansion and partial pressures → fails at low T.
Recall that b corrects for volume and a corrects for attraction in the van der Waals equation.
examNotes: The postulate-to-consequence mapping is a distinctive 5-mark question for this topic.
Explaining which postulate fails under a stated condition, such as 200 atm, is a common 2–3 mark item.
The derivation chain from PV = ⅓mnc̄² to PV = nRT is asked regularly.
Polyatomic specific heats and liquefaction are the two subtler limitations most often expected.
